title: Total Characters in String After Transformations II
summary: Given a string s consisting of lowercase English letters, an integer t representing the number of transformations to perform, and an array nums of size 26, each character in s is transformed in exactly t transformations according to the following rule: replace s[i] with the next nums[s[i] - 'a'] consecutive characters in the alphabet.
statement: Given a string s consisting of lowercase English letters, an integer t representing the number of transformations to perform, and an array nums of size 26, each character in s is transformed in exactly t transformations according to the following rule: replace s[i] with the next nums[s[i] - 'a'] consecutive characters in the alphabet. If the transformation wraps around the alphabet, it continues from the beginning. For example, if s[i] = 'y' and nums[24] = 3 , the character 'y' transforms to "zab". Return the length of the resulting string after t transformations, modulo 10^9 + 7 .
constraints: s has 1–100,000 lowercase letters, t is 1..1,000,000,000, and nums has 26 values in 1..25.
Letter i becomes the next nums[i] alphabet letters, wrapping after z.
Return the length after exactly t simultaneous transformations modulo 1,000,000,007.
hints: One transformation is a fixed 26-by-26 linear map of letter counts.
Exponentiate that transition matrix instead of applying up to one billion steps.
Build wrapped successor entries, binary-power the matrix, and multiply initial counts by the result.
Matrix composition exactly represents consecutive independent transformations; binary exponentiation reduces t steps to logarithmically many products.
editorial: Matrix composition exactly represents consecutive independent transformations; binary exponentiation reduces t steps to logarithmically many products.

tests.explanation: The first step forms bcdzz and the second forms cdeabab, of length seven.
Each of four letters produces two successors, including z wrapping to ab, so the length is eight.
